summary.text: A tropical cyclone is a rapidly rotating storm system with a low-pressure centre, strong winds and spiralling thunderstorms that bring heavy rain and squalls.
It draws its energy from water evaporating off warm seas, which later condenses into clouds and rain, unlike mid-latitude storms powered mainly by temperature contrasts.
The same kind of storm is called a hurricane in the Atlantic and northeastern Pacific, a typhoon in the northwestern Pacific, and a tropical cyclone in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

facts.label: Spin direction
facts.value: Counterclockwise north of the equator, clockwise south

items.prompt: A typhoon near Japan and a hurricane near Florida are compared side by side. What is the real difference between them?

options.label: Typhoons are always far stronger
Hurricanes spin in the opposite direction
Only the ocean region where they occur
Typhoons draw energy from land heat

items.explain: A typhoon is the same thing as a hurricane; the name depends on whether it occurs in the northwestern Pacific or the Atlantic and northeastern Pacific.

items.prompt: Why do tropical cyclones almost never form right on the equator?

options.label: The sea there is too cold
Earth's spin gives too little twist there
There is not enough moisture there
Winds there are too weak to start rain

items.explain: Their rotation comes from angular momentum imparted by Earth's rotation, so they rarely form within 5° of the equator.

items.prompt: A hurricane comes ashore and keeps moving inland over dry ground. Why does damage usually ease far from the coast?

options.label: It loses the warm ocean that powers it
Hills physically block its spinning winds
Land friction reverses its direction
Inland air is too cold for any rain

items.explain: Heat energy from the ocean acts as the accelerator for tropical cyclones, so inland regions suffer far less damage than coasts, though flooding is felt widely.

items.prompt: A storm dumps far more rain on one town over two days than the local air could ever hold at once. How is that possible?

options.label: The rain is mostly seawater thrown by waves
The town's own lakes evaporate and fall again
The air is squeezed and so holds more water
The storm keeps pulling in moist air from far away

items.explain: Tropical cyclones draw in air from a large area and concentrate its water into rain over a much smaller area, replenishing moisture again and again.

items.prompt: Warm water sits under a cluster of thunderstorms, but strong winds shear across the area at different heights. What is the likely outcome?

options.label: A cyclone forms faster than usual
The cluster struggles to grow into a cyclone
The storms turn into a blizzard
The storm spins the opposite way

items.explain: Further development needs low vertical wind shear; consistently strong shear is one reason South Atlantic cyclones are very rare.

items.prompt: Seen from space, a storm in the Southern Hemisphere spins clockwise while one in the north spins counterclockwise. What causes the difference?

options.label: Differences in ocean saltiness
The direction the trade winds blow
The Coriolis effect
The season in each hemisphere

items.explain: The opposite direction of circulation in each hemisphere is due to the Coriolis effect.
